--- title: "Census Data in Python, Part 2: Mapping with pygris and GeoPandas" subtitle: "Pulling census geometry and making choropleth maps of North Carolina" description: "Download census boundaries with pygris, join them to your Census API results, and map North Carolina counties and Mecklenburg County census tracts with GeoPandas." order: 5 --- ::: {.callout-note} ## About this tutorial **Time:** about 25 minutes. **Prerequisites:** [Census Data in Python, Part 1](census-python-part1.qmd), including the `census_helpers.py` file you saved at the end of that tutorial. By the end, you will be able to: - download county and census tract boundaries with pygris - join census data to those boundaries using the GEOID - make a choropleth map with GeoPandas and matplotlib - choose a map projection that suits North Carolina - map census tracts, remove large bodies of water, and add county outlines - make an interactive map for exploring your data ::: ## Why a second library? Polars is fast and pleasant for tables. It doesn't support geometry, though. For maps you will use [GeoPandas](https://geopandas.org){target="_blank"}, which adds a geometry column to a pandas DataFrame. You will download the shapes themselves with [pygris](https://walker-data.com/pygris/){target="_blank"}. Kyle Walker wrote pygris as the Python version of tigris, the R package that tidycensus uses to fetch boundaries. The workflow looks like this: 1. Pull the numbers from the Census API with `get_census()` from Part 1. 2. Pull the matching shapes with pygris. 3. Join the two on `GEOID`. 4. Map the result. In R, `geometry = TRUE` does steps 2 and 3 for you. In Python you do them yourself, and it takes only a few more lines. ## Setup ```bash pip install pygris geopandas matplotlib pyarrow folium mapclassify ``` GeoPandas needs `pyarrow` to receive data from Polars. `folium` and `mapclassify` are only needed for the interactive map at the end. ::: {#2ee996f8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import polars as pl from matplotlib.ticker import StrMethodFormatter from pygris import counties, tracts from pygris.utils import erase_water from census_helpers import get_census ``` ::: ## Downloading boundaries pygris has one function for each type of census geography. Let's start with North Carolina counties: ::: {#92740c8d .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} nc_shapes = counties(state="NC", cb=True, year=2024, cache=True) nc_shapes.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Using FIPS code '37' for input 'NC' ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: A few arguments deserve a note: - `cb=True` requests the **cartographic boundary** files. These are simplified shapes that draw quickly and follow the coastline. Leave it off only if you need the precise legal boundaries. - `year=2024` matches the shapes to the 2020 to 2024 ACS data you will join to them. - `cache=True` saves the files on your computer. The next request for the same shapes loads instantly. The result is a **GeoDataFrame** with 100 rows. Its `geometry` column holds each county's outline. It also has a `GEOID` column in the same format that `get_census()` produces. That shared column is what makes the join work. Check the coordinate reference system (CRS) and make a quick plot: ::: {#8d01a74d .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(nc_shapes.crs) nc_shapes.plot() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` EPSG:4269 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](census-python-part2_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-2.png){width=579 height=239} ::: ::: The CRS is EPSG 4269, called NAD83. It stores locations as longitude and latitude. ## Joining census data to shapes Get median household income for each county, just as you did in Part 1: ::: {#482727d5 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} nc_income = get_census( dataset="acs/acs5", year=2024, variables={ "median_income": "B19013_001E", "median_income_moe": "B19013_001M", }, geo_for="county:*", geo_in="state:37", ) ``` ::: GeoPandas can't merge with a Polars DataFrame directly, so convert it with `.to_pandas()` first. Keep only `GEOID` and `geometry` from the shapes. Otherwise both tables would contribute a `NAME` column and you would end up with `NAME_x` and `NAME_y`. ::: {#bb4f905d .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} nc_map = nc_shapes[["GEOID", "geometry"]].merge( nc_income.to_pandas(), on="GEOID", how="left" ) nc_map.shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` (100, 5) ``` ::: ::: Put the GeoDataFrame on the left side of the merge. The result then stays a GeoDataFrame that you can map. Using `how="left"` keeps every county even if its data is missing. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Check your join After any join, confirm that the rows matched. `nc_map["median_income"].isna().sum()` counts the counties with no data. If that number is large, compare a few GEOIDs from each table. Look for missing leading zeros, or for a GEOID that was stored as a number. ::: ## A choropleth map A **choropleth** map shades each area by the value of a variable. GeoPandas makes one with `.plot(column=...)`: ::: {#17c14078 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 5)) nc_map.plot( column="median_income", cmap="viridis", edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.2, legend=True, legend_kwds={"orientation": "horizontal", "shrink": 0.5, "pad": 0.02}, missing_kwds={"color": "lightgrey"}, ax=ax, ) ax.set_title("Median household income by county, North Carolina (2020 to 2024 ACS)") ax.set_axis_off() fig.axes[1].xaxis.set_major_formatter(StrMethodFormatter("${x:,.0f}")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](census-python-part2_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){width=828 height=399} ::: ::: Here is what each piece does: - `cmap="viridis"` uses a color scale that is easy to read for people with color vision deficiencies. - `missing_kwds` draws counties with missing data in gray. Without it, those counties would disappear from the map. - `ax.set_axis_off()` hides the longitude and latitude ticks. They rarely help a reader. - The last line formats the legend as dollars. The legend is a second set of axes, so it lives in `fig.axes[1]`. ### Choosing a projection Longitude and latitude describe points on a globe. Drawing them directly on a flat screen stretches the map a little. North Carolina has its own projected CRS, called NAD83 / North Carolina (EPSG 32119). Switch to it with `.to_crs()`: ::: {#33eb1971 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} nc_map = nc_map.to_crs(32119) ``` ::: Run the plotting code again and compare. The shapes will look more like official maps of the state. Projected coordinates are measured in meters, which also makes them the right choice for measuring areas and distances. ## Mapping census tracts The same steps work for tracts. Download Mecklenburg County's tracts and project them: ::: {#19a61e35 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} meck_shapes = tracts(state="NC", county="Mecklenburg", cb=True, year=2024, cache=True) meck_shapes = meck_shapes.to_crs(32119) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Using FIPS code '37' for input 'NC' Using FIPS code '119' for input 'Mecklenburg' ``` ::: ::: pygris accepts county names, unlike the Census API. Now get the data and join: ::: {#62aa84e7 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} meck_income = get_census( dataset="acs/acs5", year=2024, variables={ "median_income": "B19013_001E", "median_income_moe": "B19013_001M", }, geo_for="tract:*", geo_in="state:37 county:119", ) meck_map = meck_shapes[["GEOID", "geometry"]].merge( meck_income.to_pandas(), on="GEOID", how="left" ) ``` ::: ### Removing water Census tract boundaries include water. On the northern edge of Mecklenburg County, the tracts along Lake Norman extend into the lake. `erase_water()` cuts large bodies of water out of your shapes: ::: {#486c0ccb .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} meck_map = erase_water(meck_map, area_threshold=0.9, year=2024) ``` ::: The `area_threshold` argument controls how much water gets erased. A value of `0.9` removes only the largest 10 percent of water features. This step can take a minute the first time you run it. You may also see a `UserWarning` about dropped geometries. It is safe to ignore. Now make the map: ::: {#a0af7e5d .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8)) meck_map.plot( column="median_income", cmap="viridis", legend=True, legend_kwds={"shrink": 0.6}, missing_kwds={"color": "lightgrey"}, ax=ax, ) ax.set_title("Median household income by census tract, Mecklenburg County") ax.set_axis_off() fig.axes[1].yaxis.set_major_formatter(StrMethodFormatter("${x:,.0f}")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](census-python-part2_files/figure-html/cell-12-output-1.png){width=635 height=623} ::: ::: This legend is vertical, so the formatter goes on its `yaxis`. ### Mapping a region with county outlines To show tracts across several counties, download each county's tracts and stack them. Then draw county outlines on top so readers can orient themselves. You found the FIPS codes for Iredell (`097`) and Cabarrus (`025`) in Part 1. ::: {#56ea67e8 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} region_counties = ["Mecklenburg", "Iredell", "Cabarrus"] region_shapes = tracts( state="NC", county=region_counties, cb=True, year=2024, cache=True ).to_crs(32119) region_income = get_census( dataset="acs/acs5", year=2024, variables={"median_income": "B19013_001E"}, geo_for="tract:*", geo_in="state:37 county:119,097,025", ) region_map = region_shapes[["GEOID", "geometry"]].merge( region_income.to_pandas(), on="GEOID", how="left" ) region_outlines = nc_shapes[nc_shapes["NAME"].isin(region_counties)].to_crs(32119) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Using FIPS code '37' for input 'NC' Using FIPS code '119' for input 'Mecklenburg' Using FIPS code '097' for input 'Iredell' Using FIPS code '025' for input 'Cabarrus' ``` ::: ::: Plot both layers on the same axes. Use `.boundary` to draw the county outlines without filling them: ::: {#da74a4fd .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8)) region_map.plot( column="median_income", cmap="viridis", legend=True, legend_kwds={"shrink": 0.6}, missing_kwds={"color": "lightgrey"}, ax=ax, ) region_outlines.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="white", linewidth=1) ax.set_title("Median household income around Lake Norman") ax.set_axis_off() fig.axes[1].yaxis.set_major_formatter(StrMethodFormatter("${x:,.0f}")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](census-python-part2_files/figure-html/cell-14-output-1.png){width=516 height=631} ::: ::: ## Mapping several variables at once Small multiples put several maps side by side on one color scale. This example maps four racial and ethnic groups across Mecklenburg tracts from the 2020 Redistricting file. The data is from 2020, so use the 2020 tract shapes. ::: {#312771d8 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} groups = {"White": "P1_003N", "Black": "P1_004N", "Asian": "P1_006N", "Hispanic": "P2_002N"} meck_race = get_census( dataset="dec/pl", year=2020, variables={**groups, "total_pop": "P1_001N"}, geo_for="tract:*", geo_in="state:37 county:119", ).with_columns( (100 * pl.col(group) / pl.col("total_pop")).alias(group) for group in groups ) meck_race_map = ( tracts(state="NC", county="Mecklenburg", cb=True, year=2020, cache=True) .to_crs(32119)[["GEOID", "geometry"]] .merge(meck_race.to_pandas(), on="GEOID", how="left") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Using FIPS code '37' for input 'NC' Using FIPS code '119' for input 'Mecklenburg' ``` ::: ::: Loop over the groups and draw each one in its own panel. Setting `vmin` and `vmax` gives every panel the same scale, from 0 to 100 percent: ::: {#dd34e4ec .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 10)) for ax, group in zip(axes.flat, groups): meck_race_map.plot( column=group, cmap="magma_r", vmin=0, vmax=100, missing_kwds={"color": "lightgrey"}, ax=ax, ) ax.set_title(group) ax.set_axis_off() fig.colorbar( plt.cm.ScalarMappable(norm=plt.Normalize(0, 100), cmap="magma_r"), ax=axes, shrink=0.6, label="Percent of tract population", ) fig.suptitle("Race and ethnicity by census tract, Mecklenburg County (2020)") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](census-python-part2_files/figure-html/cell-16-output-1.png){width=728 height=852} ::: ::: The Census Bureau counts Hispanic origin separately from race. A Hispanic resident may also be counted in one of the race groups, so the four percentages can add up to more than 100. ## Interactive maps A static map is best for a presentation. While you explore, an interactive map lets you zoom in and hover over tracts to read their values. GeoPandas makes one with `.explore()`: ::: {#a57fac8b .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} meck_map.explore( column="median_income", cmap="viridis", tooltip=["NAME", "median_income", "median_income_moe"], tiles="Esri.WorldGrayCanvas", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ``````````{=html}
Make this Notebook Trusted to load map: File -> Trust Notebook
`````````` ::: ::: The `tiles` argument sets the basemap. Esri's World Gray Canvas is a light gray map with only faint roads and borders, so it doesn't compete with your colors. It is free and needs no API key. Leave `tiles` out to get the default OpenStreetMap street map. In a Jupyter notebook, the map appears below the cell. In a plain script, save it with `.save("meck_income.html")` and open the file in your browser. ## Attaching census shapes to other data Sometimes your data doesn't come from the Census Bureau. It might be a table of eviction filings, school test scores, or health outcomes by tract. If it has a GEOID column, the join works exactly as it did above: ::: {#ad887c63 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} my_data = pl.read_csv("my_tract_data.csv", schema_overrides={"GEOID": pl.String}) my_map = meck_shapes[["GEOID", "geometry"]].merge( my_data.to_pandas(), on="GEOID", how="left" ) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## Match your years Tract boundaries changed in 2020. Data that uses 2010 tract GEOIDs won't join cleanly to 2020 or later shapes. If many rows fail to match, check which decade's tracts your data uses. ::: ## Saving maps and shapes Save a map as an image for your slides: ::: {#8b54f0f4 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig.savefig("meck_income_map.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight") ``` ::: Save the spatial data itself as a GeoPackage. A GeoPackage keeps the shapes, the data, and the CRS together in one file. Teammates can open it in Python, in R, or in QGIS. ::: {#a9867bde .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} meck_map.to_file("meck_income.gpkg") ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## A shortcut for later pygris also includes its own `get_census()` function in `pygris.data`. It sends the request and returns a pandas DataFrame, and it can build the GEOID for you. Now that you know what happens behind the scenes, feel free to use whichever version you like. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Make a county map of the percentage of people below the poverty level in North Carolina, using the poverty data from Part 1. Project it to EPSG 32119. 2. Map the median gross rent (`B25064_001E`) for census tracts in Mecklenburg, Iredell, and Cabarrus counties. Remove the water and add county outlines. Where are rents highest? 3. Make a second map that shows the **margin of error** (`B25064_001M`) for the same rent data. Which areas have the least reliable estimates? How would you mention that in a presentation? ## Further reading - The [pygris documentation](https://walker-data.com/pygris/){target="_blank"}, including its guide to data availability by year - The [GeoPandas mapping guide](https://geopandas.org/en/stable/docs/user_guide/mapping.html){target="_blank"} and its guide to [interactive maps](https://geopandas.org/en/stable/docs/user_guide/interactive_mapping.html){target="_blank"} - Kyle Walker's [*Analyzing US Census Data*](https://walker-data.com/census-r/){target="_blank"} is written for R. [Chapter 5](https://walker-data.com/census-r/census-geographic-data-and-applications-in-r.html){target="_blank"} explains cartographic boundaries, projections, and yearly boundary changes in ways that apply to pygris too. [Chapter 6](https://walker-data.com/census-r/mapping-census-data-with-r.html){target="_blank"} is full of good advice on map design. **Using R instead?** See [Census Data in R, Part 1](census-r-part1.qmd).
